comments.author: mDuo13
comments.body:
I'd second the approach of breaking this into several separate steps with common setup steps. In fact, it's OK even if the setup steps for the later tests is very similar to the earlier tests.

Also, it might be worth creating a few different variations of the rippling setup. For example (the arrows point away from the side with the nonzero limit):

- Chained trust, Alice→Bob→Charlie. (Charlie can send a payment that ripples through Bob to Alice, even if Bob has DepositAuth, as long as Bob doesn't have NoRipple enabled on both trust lines.) Uniquely, this setup works even if you don't "send a payment so there's something to ripple first" because both Charlie and Bob are issuing from a zero balance in this case.
- Issuing gateway, Alice→Gateway←Bob. (If Gateway has previously paid Alice, and Gateway doesn't have NoRipple on both trust lines, then Alice can send a payment which ripples through Gateway to pay Bob. Also, vice-versa.)
- Market maker / Credit hub, Alice←Mark→Bob. (If Bob has previously paid Mark, and Mark doesn't have NoRipple on both trust lines, then Alice can send a payment that ripples through Mark to Bob. And vice-versa.)

Some more exotic cases I'm not sure are worth testing, but are at least worth thinking about:

- Two-way trust lines, like Alice⟷Bob (with third party on either end). Specifically, I'd want to test a payment that swaps the sign of the balance.
- Multi-part no-ripple evasion (the exploit addressed by DefaultRipple).

comments.author: scottschurr
comments.body:
@mduo13, thanks for looking at the tests.  Regarding the additional tests, do we have any reason to believe that `DepositAuth` will have any more interaction with rippling in the additional suggested scenarios than it does in the two current test cases?  My inclination is to say that the two test cases on this branch show that `DepositAuth` and rippling are independent of each other.  We see that `DepositAuth` lays no additional rippling traps, but also cures none of them.

Unless we have reason to believe that there are interactions that I've missed then I'd prefer not to add new test cases.  I could see adding rippling test cases -- independent of DepositAuth.  But those would be in another file.  And I'd like to spend some time looking at your doc review :smile:.

prs.body:
@mDuo13 asked a couple of questions about the interactions between PaymentAuth and rippling.  I didn't know the answers, so here is a unit test that I believe answers the questions:

1. If a DepositAuth'd account has created a trust line with a nonzero limit, it _can_ receive that currency via rippling in a Payment transaction as long as the Destination of said Payment is not the account.

2. If a DepositAuth'd account issues currency on a trust line, it _can_ receive that currency via rippling in a Payment transaction as long as the Destination of said Payment is not the account.

In effect, as long as the DepositAuth'd account is not the final destination of the Payment, the rules for rippling are unaffected by the presence of the DepositAuth flag.

Reviewers: @seelabs for payment rippling experience, @ximinez for hole spotting.

issues.title: IOU's/issued tokens forever blocked from sending back to issuer (Blackhole+DepositAuth)
issues.author: Wietse-Livingroom
issues.body:
## Issue Description
Issued tokens on the XRPL can normally be sent back to the issuing account. Doing so will lower the obligation by the issuer, and allow the sender to destroy tokens (lower distribution) or even fully clean out a balance. For example to be able to remove a Trust Line.

When a token is issued as an independent (non-IOU) token, it's a common practice to issue, set the Regular Key to ACCOUNT_ZERO or ACCOUNT_ONE and then disable the master key. This way the issuing account is "black holed": issuing account access is destroyed, the supply cannot be increased and Trust Lines cannot be frozen.

When, before disabling the master key of the issuing account, the `DepositAuth` flag is set with an `AccountSet` transaction (on the issuing account), the issuing account will no longer accept incoming transactions (from a non-whitelisted account). If the account is then black holed, no one will ever be able to send back issued tokens to the issuer, as those transactions will fail with a `tecNO_PERMISSION` error.

## Implications
If an issued token can no longer be returned to the issuer one can never voluntarily get rid of the token in a 'clean' way. This would leave people with a Trust Line & reserve that can never be closed & freed up again. A workaround could be to find a random other Trust  Line and send off all owned tokens there, but that's a dirty solution (especially for the random recipient). Also, if one is the only holder of the token, there is no other party to send the tokens to, resulting in an forever useless Trust Line & reserve.

## Proposed change (please discuss)
- Ignore `DepositAuth` check for incoming transactions of a token issued by the receiving account: the issuer can already block incoming transactions for issued tokens with a `Global Freeze`.
